summary: Idaho is currently legal for a captive-bred pet roof rat, but it is the state to watch. Two state regimes govern the question and neither reaches R. rattus as a pet. The Idaho State Department of Agriculture (ISDA) bans possessing a 'deleterious exotic animal,' but its enumerated list (IDAPA 02.04.27.410, under Idaho Code Title 25, Chapter 39) names specific exotic rodents (Gambian pouched rats, prairie dogs, several African genera, South American rodents) and does NOT list the genus Rattus, so no ISDA possession permit is required. Idaho Fish & Game (IDFG) regulates 'wildlife,' but its rules (IDAPA 13.01.10) classify rodents as 'Conventional Pets' that are exempt from any IDFG permit to possess, breed, or sell. So keeping, hobby-breeding, and selling or giving a captive-bred roof rat is legal at the state level. Importing any pet into Idaho from out of state requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI); a June 2026 ISDA emergency order tightens this to a 5-day CVI (and an entry permit from infested zones) for warm-blooded animals, including pet rodents, originating from New World Screwworm states. Releasing a roof rat into the wild is prohibited. Advocacy watch: in the 2026 session the Idaho Senate passed S1271, the 'Rodents of Unusual Size Act,' which named both the Norway rat and the roof rat as a public-health nuisance for statewide abatement with no carve-out for caged pets; the House defeated it 32-38 on March 17, 2026, so it is dead for the 2026 session. A successor bill could return in 2027. The keep, breed, and sell/give answers reflect current law; they would be displaced if a future ban passes.

kit.time_sensitive: S1271 is dead for the 2026 session (defeated in the House 32-38 on March 17, 2026). Watch for a 2027 successor bill and act when one is introduced, before its committee hearing.
kit.problem: Keeping a captive-bred roof rat (Rattus rattus) as a pet is currently legal in Idaho: the species is not on the ISDA deleterious-exotic-animal list (IDAPA 02.04.27.410) and rodents are exempt 'Conventional Pets' under the Fish & Game rules (IDAPA 13.01.10). In the 2026 session, Senate Bill 1271 (the 'Rodents of Unusual Size Act') would have declared the Norway rat and the roof rat a public-health nuisance, an invasive species, and an agricultural pest, and directed statewide abatement, with no exemption for caged, captive-bred pet rats. The Idaho Senate passed it 28-3-4 on March 5, 2026; the House defeated it 32-38 on March 17, 2026, so it is dead for the 2026 session. The margin and the underlying wild-rat concern in the Treasure Valley make a successor bill in 2027 plausible.
kit.ask: Ask your Idaho state legislators to oppose any future bill that bans or targets privately kept, captive-bred roof rats, and to distinguish domesticated pet Rattus rattus from wild pest populations. The fancy rat Idahoans already keep legally is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century; a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/). Cats and dogs are also non-native and documented to harm native wildlife, yet are permitted as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few tame, indoor-only, captive-bred roof rats is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a cost-benefit judgment for the Legislature. The narrow question is that trade-off, and whether any future bill can exempt securely caged, captive-bred pets while still addressing wild populations, not whether the wild species can be a pest.
kit.branch_note: This is a question of statute, not agency rule. The threat is a future law that would name the species, so the people who decide are your elected Senator and Representative, and testimony when a bill is in committee (S1271 was heard in the Senate and House Agricultural Affairs committees and decided on the House floor 32-38). Writing a state agency will not stop a bill. A secondary watch point is the ISDA, which has independent authority under Idaho Code Title 25, Chapter 39 to add a species to the deleterious-exotic list by rule; if it ever opens such a rulemaking on Rattus, the public-comment process is the place to respond.

targets.name: Find & write your Idaho State Senator and Representative
targets.why: They cast the votes on any ban. S1271 was decided on the House floor, 32-38, on March 17, 2026.

template.en:
Dear Senator / Representative [name],

I am a constituent in [town]. I am writing to ask you to oppose any bill that would ban or target privately kept, captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) as pets, such as the 2026 'Rodents of Unusual Size Act' (S1271), and to distinguish domesticated pet rats from wild pest populations in any future legislation.

Domesticated, captive-bred roof rats are not the wild pests such a bill is aimed at. They are kept in cages indoors, never released, and are no more an agricultural threat than the fancy pet rats Idahoans already keep legally. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century; a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. A blanket ban would punish responsible pet owners without affecting wild populations.

The same trade-off already applies to other pets. Cats and dogs are non-native and documented to harm native wildlife, yet are permitted because their companionship is judged worth it. The question a rodent ban raises is that same cost-benefit judgment, which belongs to you as lawmakers: whether the limited additional risk of a few tame, indoor-only pet rats justifies banning them. I do not ask you to assume any particular answer, only to weigh it, and to consider exempting securely caged, captive-bred pets while still addressing wild rat populations.

Thank you for your time,
[Your name, town]

keep.why: Two state regimes govern animal possession and neither reaches a captive-bred roof rat kept as a pet. (1) The ISDA bans possessing a 'deleterious exotic animal' without a permit (Idaho Code Title 25, Ch. 39; IDAPA 02.04.27), but the enumerated Rodentia list (IDAPA 02.04.27.410) names only specific exotic genera (Graphiurus, Funisciurus, Hybomys, Heliosciurus, Atherurus, Cricetomys, Cynomys, and all South American rodents except guinea pigs and chinchillas); the genus Rattus is absent, so no ISDA possession permit applies. (2) IDFG regulates 'wildlife' (Idaho Code Sec. 36-202) and generally requires a captive-possession permit (IDAPA 13.01.10.200), but rodents are listed 'Conventional Pets' (IDAPA 13.01.10.011.06: 'Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale... dogs, cats, ferrets, rabbits, rodents...'), and IDAPA 13.01.10.200.06 states no IDFG permit is needed to possess a conventional pet. A captive-bred roof rat fits both exemptions, so keeping one as a pet is legal with no state possession permit. Currently legal; see the 2026 S1271 advocacy watch for the legislative risk.
keep.governing_law: Idaho Code Title 25, Ch. 39 (Sec. 25-3901 to 25-3904; deleterious exotic animals); IDAPA 02.04.27.410 (Rattus not listed); Idaho Code Sec. 36-202 (wildlife); IDAPA 13.01.10.011.06 &.200.06 (rodents are exempt 'Conventional Pets').

breed.why: Hobby breeding of a captive-bred roof rat is legal and unregulated by the state. Because R. rattus is not a deleterious exotic animal, no ISDA propagation permit applies, and as a 'Conventional Pet' rodent it is exempt from the IDFG captive-wildlife/commercial-wildlife-facility regime (IDAPA 13.01.10). Idaho has no separate state pet-breeder or hobby-breeder license for small rodents. The federal Animal Welfare Act exempts businesses that breed or sell only rats, mice, or birds, so even commercial-scale rat breeding does not trigger USDA licensure. One textual ambiguity: the 'Conventional Pet' definition excludes animals 'intended for... resale,' so a strict reading could pull large-scale commercial breeding-for-resale out of the exemption and toward the IDFG 'commercial wildlife facility' rules; in practice the state treats domestic rats as pets, not wildlife, and does not apply that regime to rat breeders. Hobby breeding is clearly legal.
breed.governing_law: IDAPA 02.04.27.410 (Rattus not a deleterious exotic); IDAPA 13.01.10.011 &.200.06 (conventional-pet rodent exemption); 7 U.S.C. Sec. 2132(g)/9 C.F.R. Sec. 2.1 (AWA exemption for rats/mice/birds). No Idaho pet-breeder license for rodents.

sell_give.why: Selling or giving away a captive-bred roof rat is legal at the state level. IDAPA 13.01.10.200.06 expressly states no IDFG permit is needed to 'sell' a conventional pet, and Idaho has no state pet-dealer license reaching private rodent sales or rehoming. Giving a rat away for free is unambiguously legal: there is no commercial transaction, so the animal plainly remains a 'privately owned companion animal not intended for... resale.' For paid sales there is a textual ambiguity in the IDFG rule: the 'Conventional Pet' definition (IDAPA 13.01.10.011.06) excludes animals 'intended for... resale,' which a strict reading could argue strips the exemption from an animal held for sale. In practice the retail and private sale of pet rats occurs routinely in Idaho without IDFG intervention, and the state maintains no pet-dealer licensing for rodents, so sale operates as unregulated. Confidence is medium for paid sales because of that unresolved drafting contradiction; free rehoming is high.
sell_give.governing_law: IDAPA 13.01.10.200.06 (no permit to sell a conventional pet) &.011.06 (conventional-pet definition with 'resale' exclusion); IDAPA 02.04.27.410 (Rattus not a deleterious exotic); no Idaho pet-dealer license for rodents.

transport.why: Moving a roof rat within Idaho is legal and unregulated (a conventional pet is exempt from IDFG transport permits under IDAPA 13.01.10.200.06). Importing one into Idaho from out of state is regulated by the ISDA: under the Rules Governing the Importation of Animals (IDAPA 02.04.21), all animals entering Idaho must be accompanied by an official Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI), normally issued within 30 days, and ISDA's household-pet import guidance confirms small pets/rodents require at least a CVI. A June 2026 ISDA emergency order in response to New World Screwworm tightens this for warm-blooded animals (expressly including companion animals) from affected states: a CVI issued within 5 days of entry, plus an ISDA entry permit if the animal originates from a designated infested zone. The deleterious-exotic import ban does not reach R. rattus. Releasing a roof rat into the wild is prohibited (it is a non-native species; the IDFG release exemption covers only native wildlife).
transport.governing_law: IDAPA 02.04.21 (importation of animals; CVI requirement); ISDA household-pet import guidance (CVI for rodents/small furries); ISDA Administrative Order of June 9, 2026 (New World Screwworm: 5-day CVI / entry permit for warm-blooded animals incl. pets); IDAPA 13.01.10.200.06 (intrastate transport of conventional pet exempt); IDAPA 02.04.27.410 (deleterious import ban N/A to Rattus).

restrictions.summary: Importing a roof rat into Idaho from another state requires an official Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI), normally issued within 30 days, listing the Idaho destination address. Under the June 2026 ISDA New World Screwworm emergency order, warm-blooded animals (including pet rodents) from affected states need a CVI issued within 5 days of entry, and an ISDA entry permit if from a designated infested zone. No paperwork is required to move a rat within Idaho. Never release a roof rat into the wild.
steps: Before importing, have an accredited origin-state veterinarian issue an official CVI showing the Idaho destination address (standard validity 30 days)
If the animal originates from a New World Screwworm state, obtain a CVI within 5 days of entry; if from a designated infested zone, also obtain an ISDA entry permit
Confirm current pet-rodent import requirements with ISDA Animal Industries (rodents are not separately enumerated on the household-pet page)
No CVI or permit is required to move the rat within Idaho
Never release a roof rat into the wild (non-native species; release is prohibited)

restrictions.summary: Legislative watch: 2026 Senate Bill S1271 ('Rodents of Unusual Size Act') would have declared the Norway rat and the roof rat a public-health nuisance for statewide abatement, with no exemption for caged pet rats. The Senate passed it 28-3-4 (Mar 5, 2026); the House defeated it 32-38 (Mar 17, 2026), so it is dead for the 2026 session. A successor bill could return in 2027. Idaho keepers should monitor the Legislature and be ready to testify that a captive-bred pet is not a wild pest, and to ask that any future bill exempt securely caged, captive-bred pets. The ISDA also has standalone authority (Idaho Code Title 25, Ch. 39) to add a species to the deleterious-exotic list by rule; no such rulemaking on Rattus has been initiated. Check local ordinances too.
steps: Monitor the Idaho Legislature for a re-introduced rodent bill (successor to S1271), especially in the Senate and House Agricultural Affairs committees
If a bill is introduced, contact your Senator and Representative and sign up to testify at the committee hearing (captive-bred pet vs. wild pest; ask for a caged-pet carve-out)
Watch for any ISDA rulemaking to add Rattus to the IDAPA 02.04.27 deleterious-exotic list and comment if it opens
Check city/county ordinances for any local pet limits

inquiry_focus: Idaho is currently LEGAL (no inquiry strictly required); advocacy is a legislative watch, not an agency lever. Two clarifications would resolve residual ambiguity if pursued: (1) IDFG - the 'resale paradox' in IDAPA 13.01.10 (the rule exempts the 'sale' of conventional pets, but defines a conventional pet as 'not intended for resale'); does breeding-for-sale strip the conventional-pet exemption and require a Commercial Wildlife Facility license, or does IDFG exempt domestic pet-rat sales from wildlife oversight in practice? (2) ISDA - after S1271 failed, has the department opened any rulemaking to add Rattus to the IDAPA 02.04.27 deleterious-exotic list?
